input: whats it called when threads wait on a list until another thread signals something changed
expected_output: That is a condition variable. It is an explicit queue that threads put themselves on when some state is not as desired. Another thread that changes that state can then wake one or more of the waiting threads so they can continue.

evidence.quote: A condition variable is an explicit queue that threads can put themselves on when some state of execution (i.e., some condition) is not as desired (by waiting on the condition);
some other thread, when it changes said state, can then wake one (or more) of those waiting threads and thus allow them to continue (by signaling on the condition).

input: what's a spurious wakeup? i saw it mentioned somewhere in pthreads stuff and have no idea what it means
expected_output: A spurious wakeup is when, in some thread packages and due to implementation details, two threads get woken up even though only a single signal took place. Because of this, a thread should re-check the condition it is waiting on, which is one more reason to use a while loop around the check.

evidence.quote: In some thread packages, due to details of the implementation, it is possible that two threads get woken up though just a single signal has taken place
Spurious wakeups are further reason to re-check the condition a thread is waiting on.
Using while loops around conditional checks also handles the case where spurious wakeups occur.

input: Why must a lock be passed into the call that blocks a thread on a condition, and what happens to that lock while the thread sleeps and when it wakes?
expected_output: The wait call assumes the mutex is already locked when it is called. It atomically releases the lock and puts the caller to sleep, and when the thread is woken it re-acquires the lock before returning to the caller. This design exists to prevent certain race conditions when a thread is putting itself to sleep.

evidence.quote: it assumes that this mutex is locked when wait() is called.

The responsibility of wait() is to release the lock and put the calling thread to sleep (atomically); when the thread wakes up (after some other thread has signaled it), it must re-acquire the lock before returning to the caller.
This complexity stems from the desire to prevent certain race conditions from occurring when a thread is trying to put itself to sleep.

input: why does the final bounded buffer use a bunch of slots instead of just one, does that actually help anything
expected_output: Adding more buffer slots lets multiple values be produced before a producer sleeps and multiple values be consumed before a consumer sleeps. With one producer and one consumer that reduces context switches, and with several producers or consumers it also allows producing or consuming to happen concurrently, increasing concurrency.

evidence.quote: we add more buffer slots, so that multiple values can be produced before sleeping, and similarly multiple values can be consumed before sleeping.

With just a single producer and consumer, this approach is more efficient as it reduces context switches; with multiple producers or consumers (or both), it even allows concurrent producing or consuming to take place, thus increasing concurrency.

After the producer wakes the first consumer, a second consumer can sneak in and take the single value, so when the first consumer runs it calls get() on an empty buffer and an assertion triggers. now consumer Tc1 wakes up and (with the lock held) immediately re-checks the state of the shared variable (c2). If the buffer is empty at that point, the consumer simply goes back to sleep (c3).
Fortunately, this fix is easy (Figure 30.8): change the if to a while.

input: why do all my threads end up asleep with one condition variable, and whats the fix
expected_output: With a single condition variable, a consumer that has just emptied the buffer signals and may wake another consumer instead of the producer. That consumer finds the buffer empty and goes back to sleep, leaving the producer and both consumers all asleep. The fix is two condition variables: producers wait on empty and signal fill, while consumers wait on fill and signal empty, so a consumer can never wake a consumer or a producer wake a producer.

evidence.quote: However, if it wakes the consumer Tc2 (which is definitely possible, depending on how the wait queue is managed), we have a problem.
The producer Tp, which has a value to put into the buffer, is left sleeping. The other consumer thread, Tc1, also goes back to sleep. All three threads are left sleeping, a clear bug
In the code above, producer threads wait on the condition empty, and signals fill. Conversely, consumer threads wait on fill and signal empty.
Because the consumer has emptied the buffer, it clearly should wake the producer.
Specifically, the consumer Tc2 will wake up and find the buffer empty (c2), and go back to sleep (c3).
By doing so, the second problem above is avoided by design: a consumer can never accidentally wake a consumer, and a producer can never accidentally wake a producer.

input: How does broadcasting to a condition differ from signaling it, and what is the tradeoff?
expected_output: Signal is used to wake a sleeping thread waiting on the condition, whereas broadcast wakes up all waiting threads. Broadcast guarantees that any thread that should be woken is, but the cost can be a performance hit, since many other waiting threads may be needlessly woken even though they should not yet be awake.

evidence.quote: the signal() call is executed when a thread has changed something in the program and thus wants to wake a sleeping thread waiting on this condition.

pthread cond broadcast(), which wakes up all waiting threads. By doing so, we guarantee that any threads that should be woken are. The downside, of course, can be a negative performance impact, as we might needlessly wake up many other waiting threads that shouldn’t (yet) be awake.

input: so whats the deal with mesa vs hoare semantics, which one do real systems actually use?
expected_output: Under Mesa semantics a signal only wakes a thread and acts as a hint that the state has changed, with no guarantee the state is still as desired when the woken thread runs. Hoare semantics is harder to build but gives a stronger guarantee that the woken thread runs immediately. Virtually every system ever built uses Mesa semantics.

evidence.quote: Signaling a thread only wakes them up; it is thus a hint that the state of the world has changed (in this case, that a value has been placed in the buffer), but there is no guarantee that when the woken thread runs, the state will still be as desired.
the contrast, referred to as Hoare semantics, is harder to build but provides a stronger guarantee that the woken thread will run immediately upon being woken
Virtually every system ever built employs Mesa semantics.
This interpretation of what a signal means is often referred to as Mesa semantics, after the first research that built a condition variable in such a manner [LR80];

input: buffer has 5 slots and only 3 are full, does a consumer wait or just grab one?
expected_output: With 3 of 5 slots filled the buffer is not entirely empty, so the consumer does not sleep and goes ahead and takes a value. A consumer only sleeps when all buffers are empty.

evidence.quote: A producer only sleeps if all buffers are currently filled (p2); similarly, a consumer only sleeps if all buffers are currently empty (c2).

input: if i pipe grep into wc to count lines, whos the producer and consumer and whats in between
expected_output: The grep process is the producer and the wc process is the consumer, and between them is an in-kernel bounded buffer. The UNIX shell redirects grep's output to a UNIX pipe, created by the pipe system call, whose other end feeds wc.

evidence.quote: the UNIX shell redirects the output to what is called a UNIX pipe (created by the pipe system call).
Thus, the grep process is the producer; the wc process is the consumer; between them is an in-kernel bounded buffer
The other end of this pipe is connected to the standard input of the process wc, which simply counts the number of lines in the input stream and prints out the result.

input: isnt just spinning on a flag until the child is done totally fine?
expected_output: No. Spinning on a shared variable will generally work, but it is hugely inefficient because the parent spins and wastes CPU time, and in some cases it can even be incorrect. What you want instead is a way to put the parent to sleep until the condition becomes true.

evidence.quote: This solution will generally work, but it is hugely inefficient as the parent spins and wastes CPU time.
What we would like here instead is some way to put the parent to sleep until the condition we are waiting for (e.g., the child is done executing) comes true.
The simple approach, of just spinning until the condition becomes true, is grossly inefficient and wastes CPU cycles, and in some cases, can be incorrect.

input: if the child signals before the parent calls wait, the signal just gets saved right?
expected_output: No, a signal is not saved. If the child signals when no thread is asleep on the condition, nothing is woken, and when the parent later calls wait it is stuck because no thread will ever wake it. That is why you need a state variable like done, which records the value the threads care about.

evidence.quote: Imagine the case where the child runs immediately and calls thr exit() immediately; in this case, the child will signal, but there is no thread asleep on the condition. When the parent runs, it will simply call wait and be stuck; no thread will ever wake it.
From this example, you should appreciate the importance of the state variable done; it records the value the threads are interested in knowing.

input: If a concurrent program hangs unless every signal is swapped for a broadcast, though the logic shouldn't need it, what does that suggest? Is broadcast ever the right choice?
expected_output: It suggests you probably have a bug, and you should fix it rather than rely on broadcast. However, in cases like the memory allocator, where the waker cannot tell which waiting thread to wake, broadcast may be the most straightforward solution available.

evidence.quote: In general, if you find that your program only works when you change your signals to broadcasts (but you don’t think it should need to), you probably have a bug; fix it! But in cases like the memory allocator above, broadcast may be the most straightforward solution available.

input: what actually breaks if i skip taking the mutex around the done check and the wait/signal calls?
expected_output: A race condition. The parent can see done is 0 and decide to sleep, but get interrupted just before waiting; the child then sets done to 1 and signals, but no thread is waiting so nobody is woken, and the parent later sleeps forever. So hold the lock when calling signal or wait.

evidence.quote: But just before it calls wait to go to sleep, the parent is interrupted, and the child runs. The child changes the state variable done to 1 and signals, but no thread is waiting and thus no thread is woken. When the parent runs again, it sleeps forever, which is sad.
the generalization of this tip is correct: hold the lock when calling signal or wait, and you will always be in good shape.
Specifically, if the parent calls thr join() and then checks the value of done, it will see that it is 0 and thus try to go to sleep.
